project.title: 3 TERRIFYING TRUE UFO Encounters That Can't Be Explained
project.style: Calm, realistic, first-person, slow-burn, atmospheric late-night storytelling
project.narration_notes: Read in a steady, grounded voice. Let the tension build through ordinary details, pauses, and the growing sense that something is slightly wrong before it becomes impossible to dismiss.

stories.title: The Light Over the Service Road

segments.visual_prompt: Lonely rural service road at night, utility poles, empty fields, dashboard glow inside an older sedan, realistic cinematic darkness
segments.narration: I used to take the service road home because it cut fifteen minutes off the drive and almost nobody used it after dark. It ran behind warehouses, past open fields and a drainage canal. During the day it looked dull enough to forget. At night it felt unfinished, like a road built for traffic that never came.

segments.visual_prompt: Single pale light hovering above field beside road, seen through windshield, no visible aircraft structure, faint mist near ground
segments.narration: I was twenty-six, working late shifts at a printing plant. That night I left after one and turned onto the service road as usual. About halfway down, I noticed a light above the fields to my left. It wasn't blinking. It wasn't moving. Just hanging there, low over the field at a height that felt wrong for a star and too still for an aircraft.

segments.visual_prompt: Driver pulled onto gravel shoulder, pale oval object suspended silently over field, no beam, no sound, dashboard clock glowing 1:17 AM
segments.narration: I pulled onto the shoulder and rolled the window down. No rotor noise. No engine. Nothing. The light was white with a faint bluish edge, attached to something solid — an oval shape, smooth, no visible wings. I checked the clock. It was 1:17. When I looked again it was 1:24. I was sitting upright with both hands on the wheel. I hadn't blacked out. Seven minutes were just gone.

segments.visual_prompt: Object gliding silently sideways across field without turning, then rising straight upward into cloud cover, driver frozen in car
segments.narration: Then it moved — sideways across the field in one smooth motion, no tilt, no turn, the way a reflection slides across glass. That was when my brain stopped trying to explain it. It stopped over the canal and rose straight up. No acceleration curve. One second it was low over the water. The next it was gone.

segments.visual_prompt: Empty night sky over field, driver gripping steering wheel, cold coffee in cup holder, unresolved darkness
segments.narration: The field looked normal again immediately, which somehow made it worse. No smoke, no noise, no sign anything had happened. Just wet grass and my coffee gone cold. I kept using the highway after that, even though it took longer. I still don't know what it was. I only know what I saw — a silent object moving in a way no aircraft should, and seven minutes I still can't account for.

segments.visual_prompt: Quiet suburban backyard at night, above-ground pool, fence lines, family patio light, late summer atmosphere
segments.narration: The summer I was thirteen, my parents rented a house at the end of a cul-de-sac that backed onto undeveloped land. It wasn't rural, but at night the tree line behind the fences turned into one long black wall, and once people went inside, the whole street went strangely still. We lived there eleven months. Only one night from that year stayed with every member of my family in exactly the same way.

segments.visual_prompt: Family in backyard after dinner, warm porch light, children looking upward, father stopping mid-task and staring
segments.narration: It was late August, warm enough to eat outside. My father was stacking plates, my mother wiping the table. My younger sister pointed above the tree line and asked why a star was moving so low. My father barely looked up at first. Then he stopped what he was doing and just stared.

segments.visual_prompt: Metallic object hovering above backyard tree line, dull surface with evenly spaced pale lights on underside, dog backing toward patio door
segments.narration: The object was metallic and low, sitting just above the treetops. A few steady lights along the underside — pale, evenly spaced, no blinking, no navigation colors. No sound at all. What I remember most is the dog. Usually excitable about everything. That night he went completely still, then started whining and backing toward the door without taking his eyes off the tree line.

segments.visual_prompt: Object shifting in precise stop-start bursts across neighboring yards, neighbor stepping outside and looking up, suburban rooftops below
segments.narration: It moved in short, precise bursts — perfectly still for several seconds, then relocating sideways over two or three backyards with no visible transition. It didn't drift. It just appeared elsewhere. Our neighbor came outside, looked up, and covered her mouth. She and her husband saw the same thing we did. Then it tilted, rose fast enough that my sister screamed, and vanished. Not into the distance. Just gone.

segments.visual_prompt: Suburban backyard under stars, empty sky above tree line, family standing stunned, dog pressed against patio door
segments.narration: There was nothing on the news. No explanation from the airport. No article anywhere. The event just sat in our family history with nowhere to go. What stays with me isn't only the object. It's that five people and a very frightened dog all reacted before anyone had time to build a story around it. We saw something that behaved like no aircraft we knew, made no sound, and left so abruptly that the memory still feels like a gap cut out of an ordinary summer night.

stories.title: The Object That Stayed Too Long

segments.visual_prompt: Small upstairs bedroom at night, wide window facing dark treeline, digital alarm clock glowing 2:13 AM, pale light seeping through curtain gap
segments.narration: I was nineteen, staying in my uncle's upstairs room between semesters. It faced a patch of woods and had one of those wide old windows that made everything outside feel closer at night. I liked the quiet there. No traffic, no apartment noise. Just insects in summer, and wind in the trees when the weather changed.

segments.visual_prompt: Curtain pulled back slightly, bright circular object hovering beyond treeline, brighter at edges, darker in center, silent night
segments.narration: Around two in the morning the room felt brighter than it should. I pulled the curtain back and saw an object beyond the tree line at about the height of the taller pines — circular, bright around the edges and darker in the center, like a hole cut into the night with light around it. It wasn't close enough to light up the yard. But it was bright enough to catch the window frame.

segments.visual_prompt: Bedroom interior with alarm clock ticking minutes, witness at window, object remaining fixed in same position, insects silent outside
segments.narration: What unsettled me wasn't just that it was there. It was that it stayed. Most strange lights make sense if you watch long enough — aircraft, satellites, something on a distant hill. This didn't drift, blink, or fade. I stood there for several minutes checking the clock twice. The object held exactly the same position relative to the trees. And somewhere during that time, the insects outside went completely silent.

segments.visual_prompt: Object suddenly closer and larger in window frame without visible travel, bedroom washed in pale light, witness stepping back from glass
segments.narration: Then something happened I still can't describe cleanly. I didn't see it move. I only know that at one point it was beyond the trees, and at another it appeared larger — higher in the window — as if the distance between us had shortened with no motion in between. The room grew brighter for a few seconds. I had the distinct feeling that whatever was outside wasn't just present. It was aware of the house. Maybe aware of me specifically.

segments.visual_prompt: Uncle and witness watching object rise slowly above treetops and disappear into cloud cover, morning woods ordinary and silent
segments.narration: I finally woke my uncle. By the time we got back upstairs it had retreated to the tree line, but he saw it too. We watched it rise slowly until it disappeared behind cloud cover. No burst of speed. No dramatic exit. It left like it had all the time in the world. The next morning the woods looked completely normal. No marks, no broken branches. Nothing that would let us reduce the night to something manageable.
